html:
Portuguese East Africa was the string of Portuguese forts, towns and estates along the coast of south-east Africa that grew into the colony of Mozambique. The map shows it from 1650 to 1900.

Vasco da Gama reached this coast in 1498. Portugal soon built forts at Sofala, to tap the gold trade from the Zimbabwe plateau, and on the Island of Mozambique, which became the capital. Traders and soldiers went up the Zambezi to Sena and Tete to deal with the Mutapa kings.

For most of this period Portuguese rule was thin:

  • It was run from Goa in India until 1752.
  • Along the Zambezi, Portuguese and Afro-Portuguese families held huge estates called prazos, with private armies of slaves, and acted almost as independent lords.
  • The Rozvi drove them off the plateau in the 1690s.
  • Ivory, then enslaved people, were the main exports.

In the south, Portugal held only a post at Delagoa Bay. After the Berlin Conference of 1884, it pushed inland, defeated the Gaza kingdom in 1895 and made Lourenço Marques (now Maputo) the capital in 1898. The colony became independent as Mozambique in 1975.
sum: Portuguese East Africa was the string of Portuguese forts, towns and estates along the coast of south-east Africa that grew into the colony of Mozambique. The map shows it from 1650 to 1900.
